options.misconception: assumes a known addressee for a general invitation

options.text: A quotation from an earlier keeper, since the phrase appears in an older notebook.
options.misconception: reads the opening as a quotation from the past

options.text: A caption, since it labels the volume before the entries begin.
options.misconception: treats the opening line as a label

questions.explanation: An apostrophe addresses someone directly, and the phrase aims itself at whoever will hold the book after the writer. The reader is positioned as a successor, so the following entries read as a handover.
questions.hint: Look at who the words are aimed at.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of continuous verse with no stanza divisions.
questions.stem: The apiary book's verse moves in paragraphs with no stanza divisions at all. What follows?

options.text: The reader cannot tell where one idea ends and another begins in the logbook.
options.misconception: infers confusion from the absence of divisions

options.text: The paragraph form proves the passage is a note to a neighbour rather than a poem.
options.misconception: infers genre from the absence of stanzas

options.text: The reader moves continuously, so the lyric keeps the feel of an ongoing speech.
The verse is weaker, because poetry is only poetry when it is broken into stanzas.
options.misconception: makes stanzas a requirement for poetry

questions.explanation: Continuous verse keeps the reader moving without a break, which suits a lyric that reads as speech in progress. The absence of stanzas removes one structural signal but not the flow of the utterance.
questions.hint: Think about the pace of the reading.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a prose-form entry in a logbook is still verse.
questions.stem: Explain why the logbook's prose poem is verse rather than a note in prose.

answer.exemplar: The entry is verse because the writer's choices in it go beyond what reporting requires. The images are selected and ordered so that they build, the sentences repeat structures to hold the reader in a rhythm, and the pace changes exactly where the feeling changes. A note would have reported the loss of the colony and stopped there; this text keeps working on the reader after the facts are spent, which is the test a prose poem must pass.

questions.explanation: The entry is verse because it does more than report. Selected images, repeated structures and shifting pace keep working on the reader after the facts are spent, which is the test a prose poem must pass.
questions.hint: Ask what the passage does after the facts.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether the absence of line breaks weakens a prose poem.
questions.stem: Assess whether the prose poem's lack of line breaks weakens it against the printed verse.

options.text: Yes, because readers need line breaks to know when a thought has finished.
options.misconception: assumes readers need breaks to understand

options.text: Yes, because the form is only useful for poems that describe work and weather.
options.misconception: restricts the form to documentary subjects

options.text: No, because any poem without line breaks is stronger than one with them.
options.misconception: claims a general superiority of prose over verse

options.text: No, because the concentration of images and the shaping of clauses carry the effect without breaks.

questions.explanation: The absence of line breaks removes one device but nothing essential, because concentrated images and shaped clauses still do the work. Judging the form by breaks alone misses where the poetry actually sits.
questions.hint: Look past the missing breaks.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Prose poem identified in a passage
questions.learningObjective: Identify the patterning that makes a log entry a prose poem.

stimulus.body: 'For three weeks I have opened the boxes and found no queen and no eggs. The bees go about the work with a kind of settled sadness, the way a room is tidied by someone who is not coming back. I have read the same books twice and written nothing until now.'

questions.stem: The passage above describes a queenless colony after weeks of searching. What does it demonstrate?

options.text: It is a practical report, since every statement in it can be checked against the hives.
options.misconception: ignores the figurative language in a factual frame

options.text: It is a prose poem, because the images and the rhythms are shaped far beyond the facts reported.
It is an elegy, because it mourns the missing queen without naming her loss directly.
options.misconception: treats any sadness in a record as an elegy

options.text: It is a letter, because the closing sentence is addressed to somebody reading.
options.misconception: reads a first-person statement as a letter

questions.explanation: The passage reports facts and then reaches beyond them. The image of a room tidied by someone who will not come back, carried on one long clause, shows shaping language, which makes it a prose poem.
questions.hint: Look at the image, not just the facts.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how line breaks make a recorded loss harder to skip past.
questions.stem: Explain how the beekeeper's line breaks make the loss harder to ignore.

options.text: They make the record longer, so the loss occupies more of the page and cannot be missed.
options.misconception: reduces the effect to physical space taken up

options.text: They hold the reader at the point of the loss, so the grief is met in small, unavoidable units.
They hide the writer's sorrow, because short lines keep the feelings small and contained.
options.misconception: reads shorter lines as emotional restraint

options.text: They allow the writer to add more observations, so more detail stands in for feeling.
options.misconception: claims detail substitutes for emotional effect

questions.explanation: Lineation controls how much a reader takes in at once. Short lines at the moment of the loss make the reader meet the grief in small units, so it cannot be skimmed past.
questions.hint: Think about the size of each unit.
